content: A generic drug is a pharmaceutical product that is manufactured and distributed without the protection of a patent. It must contain the same active ingredients as the original branded formulation. In most cases, generic drugs are considered bioequivalent to their brand-name counterparts, meaning they exhibit similar pharmacokinetic (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) and pharmacodynamic (biological effects) properties. Consequently, generic drugs are assumed to be identical in terms of dosage, strength, route of administration, safety, efficacy, and intended use. Generic drugs typically become available only after the patent protections granted to the original developer have expired. Once generics enter the market, competition often drives down the prices of both the original brand-name product and the generic versions. The time it takes for a generic drug to appear on the market varies. While drug patents provide 20 years of protection, this period often begins before clinical trials, leaving the effective patent life for a drug between 7 and 12 years. The lower cost of generic drugs is primarily due to the reduced expenses incurred by generic manufacturers. These companies do not bear the high costs of drug discovery and development, which can amount to as much as $800 million for a new drug, though this figure is debated. Instead, generic manufacturers reverse-engineer known drug compounds to produce bioequivalent versions. They are not required to conduct extensive clinical trials to prove safety and efficacy, as these trials have already been completed by the original brand-name company. Instead, they must demonstrate bioequivalence to the existing drug to gain regulatory approval. Generic drugs are significantly more affordable, making them accessible to many developing countries. For instance, Thailand imports millions of generic pills of Plavix, a blood-thinning medication, from India at a cost of just 3 US cents per pill. India is a leading manufacturer of generic drugs. Generic manufacturers also benefit from the prior marketing efforts of brand-name companies, such as advertising, drug representative presentations, and free sample distribution. Many generic drugs have been on the market for years under their branded names, making them familiar to both patients and healthcare providers. When a pharmaceutical company first markets a drug, it is typically protected by a patent that grants exclusive rights to sell the drug. Generic drugs can be legally produced under specific conditions: when the patent has expired, when the generic company certifies that the brand-name patent is invalid or unenforceable, when the drug was never patented, or in countries where the patent is not in force. Once a patent expires, any pharmaceutical company can manufacture and sell the drug. Since the drug has already been tested and approved, the cost of manufacturing the generic version is a fraction of the original development and testing costs. Brand-name drug companies often employ strategies to extend their market exclusivity and delay generic competition. This may involve aggressive litigation to preserve or extend patent protection, a practice sometimes referred to as evergreening. Companies may also seek new patents on specific forms of the drug, such as single enantiomers, different inactive components, or specific hydrate forms. If granted, these patents reset the clock on patent expiration. However, these patents can later be challenged for invalidation by generic manufacturers. In some cases, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) offers a 180-day exclusivity period to the first generic manufacturer that successfully challenges a patent. During this period, only one or a few generic manufacturers can produce the drug. This exclusivity acts as a reward for the generic company willing to take on the risks and costs of patent litigation. However, this period can be controversial, as a generic producer may not immediately produce the drug but can still block other generics from entering the market. To ensure bioequivalence, most countries require generic drug manufacturers to demonstrate that their formulation is equivalent to the innovator product. While generic drugs are generally less expensive and can save patients and insurance companies significant costs, some doctors and patients believe that certain generics are not as effective as their brand-name counterparts. This perception underscores the need for more clinical studies on a drug-by-drug basis. An example of the complexities surrounding generics is warfarin, which was only available under the trade name Coumadin in North America until recently. Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic window and requires frequent blood tests to avoid subtherapeutic or toxic levels. A study in Ontario, Canada, found that replacing Coumadin with generic warfarin was safe. However, many physicians remain hesitant to switch their patients to generic equivalents. The FDA requires generic drugs to be approved through an Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA), which demonstrates therapeutic equivalence to a previously approved reference listed drug. Once approved, the FDA lists the generic drug in its Orange Book, which annotates equivalence between the reference drug and the generic. The FDA also recognizes drugs with the same active ingredients but different bioavailability, dividing them into therapeutic equivalence groups. For example, diltiazem hydrochloride has multiple equivalence groups, each considered equivalent only within its group.
